artifact.title: Improve User Activation by Finding the Friction First
artifact.content:
# Improve User Activation by Finding the Friction First

When users sign up but fail to reach value, adding more onboarding steps may not help. **Start by finding what is stopping them.** Map the journey, locate the biggest drop-offs, and ask users what they expected and why they stopped. Combine those answers with funnel data to decide what to test. [S1] [S3] [S4]

LogMeIn shows why diagnosis matters. After more than ten tests failed to improve a 90% drop-off at download, the team asked registrants why they had not downloaded. Some doubted the product was really free. Offering a choice between a paid trial and a clearly marked free version made the offer more credible and improved downloads by 300%. The lesson is not to copy that fix, but to investigate the barrier users actually face. [S1] [S2]

## Define activation as a meaningful taste of value

Choose an experience-based milestone that suggests users have received meaningful value, then check whether it correlates with long-term retention. A milestone such as using a product 100 times may be too far downstream to guide onboarding. There may be multiple plausible activation moments, so treat the metric as a hypothesis, not a universal rule. [S8]

Airtable’s week-four multi-user activity—more than one team member active and contributing to a workflow—was highly correlated with retention. This illustrates why a specific, harder-to-reach milestone can be useful when it represents meaningful use. The right measure depends on the product. [S10] [S11]

## Make the next step easier

As a practical synthesis of the evidence, work through this sequence:

- **Find the barrier:** identify the biggest drop-off and ask users what prevented them from continuing. [S1] [S3] [S4]
- **Set a value milestone:** choose an experience-based activation event and check its relationship to retention. [S8]
- **Reduce effort to get started:** make the benefit clear and offer a warm start, such as a relevant template or sample. [S3] [S5]
- **Test a focused change:** keep mandatory steps limited; a few targeted questions or one or two examples may help users take the next action. [S6] [S7]

Miro’s onboarding, for example, uses a few targeted questions to guide users to a template so they can begin within about five minutes. [S6]

**Next step:** investigate your largest activation drop-off and test one change against a milestone tied to retention. This is a starting point, not a formula: activation measures and effective onboarding vary by product. [S3] [S8] [S7]

artifact.title: Product Retention
artifact.content:
# Product Retention: Improve the Experience That Brings Customers Back

Retention is not a notification problem by default. It is the cumulative result of what customers experience and the value they receive. When people stop returning, the most useful first question may not be “How do we remind them?” but “Where does the product fail to deliver?” In marketplaces, that can mean insufficient supply or poor interactions with suppliers. [S1]

**Start by improving the path to value.** Early onboarding is a promising opportunity: it can show new users why the product matters and help them experience that value. Look for new customers having an unexpectedly poor first week or month, then investigate the experience behind it. Avoid simply copying behaviors associated with your best users; those behaviors may correlate with retention without causing it. [S2, S8]

A practical retention review can cover:
- **Core experience:** Identify journey friction or weak value, rather than defaulting to more email or push notifications. [S1]
- **Activation:** Help the right users reach a valuable first experience. [S7]
- **Workflow fit:** Consider whether the product is used often enough, or fits into a workflow or collaboration, to support repeat use. Monthly-use products may not readily become habits. [S3, S12]
- **Avoidable churn:** Review payment failures, cancellation flows, and offboarding. These tactical issues may represent 25–40% of churn after product-market fit, according to Patrick Campbell. [S5]

The practical synthesis: improve the product’s lasting value and remove preventable obstacles to staying. **One next step:** map the early customer journey and identify one point where users fail to reach value. The evidence here offers useful directions, not a universal retention formula; product frequency and the causes of churn differ. [S1, S2, S3, S5]

artifact.title: Product Growth Starts With Value—and Scales Through Learning
artifact.content:
# Product Growth Starts With Value—and Scales Through Learning

Growth is not a substitute for a product people want. It is the work of helping users reach a product’s value—and then learning how to do that more effectively and at greater scale. When growth is reduced to moving isolated metrics, teams can add friction without improving the overall user experience. [S1]

That distinction matters most when a company is deciding what to fix first. **Growth can amplify product-market fit; it cannot repair a weak product or go-to-market strategy.** Strong retention or a promising growth loop can be signs that a product is ready for more deliberate growth work. But pushing a product that does not satisfy users’ needs can expose more people to a bad experience and discourage them from returning. [S4] [S5]

## Make experimentation a learning system

Product growth rarely depends on one perfect idea. In one example, a team kept a list of 100 hypotheses and worked through them in batches of 10 during sprint cycles. The principle is to make small changes, observe what happens, and use the results to choose what to try next. Some ideas will fail; those failures can still teach the team what does not work. [S3]

The arithmetic in that example illustrates why both pace and quality matter: testing 20 ideas at a 20% success rate produces four successful ideas; raising the success rate to 30% produces six. That is 50% more successful output in the same amount of time, alongside learning from unsuccessful tests. Faster prototyping can also help teams visualize bolder ideas and gather feedback before committing. [S3] [S1]

**Practical application (synthesis):** Keep a visible list of growth hypotheses, test a manageable batch, and review both outcomes and lessons. The goal is not simply to ship more; it is to build a repeatable cycle of testing and improvement.

## Let useful product actions create discovery

Some products can grow because using them naturally introduces them to potential new users. In PayPal’s example, sending money gives the recipient a reason to create an account. Dropbox sharing similarly makes the recipient aware of the product and may help activate them. The Dropbox team worked on both the sender’s and recipient’s experiences, connecting product quality to acquisition rather than treating sharing as a detached promotional feature. [S2] [S13]

This mechanism has a limit: **a referral feature cannot replace a valuable product experience.** Slack’s early word of mouth, as described in the evidence, came from users finding the product remarkable, not from a built-in sharing mechanism. Likewise, smoothing a conversion step may produce some growth, but recommendation requires an experience users find unexpectedly valuable. [S6] [S7]

**Practical application (synthesis):** Ask whether a normal, valuable use of the product creates a natural reason for another person to encounter it. If so, improve the experience for both the existing user and the person they bring in. If not, do not force a viral mechanism that does not fit the product.

## Scale what works, but do not depend on only one engine

Early growth may begin with non-scalable efforts led by founders. These “kindle” strategies can help attract initial users and reveal whether a scalable “fire” strategy—such as content, sales, viral loops, or paid acquisition—can work. A full-time growth hire is most useful once the company has found a scalable strategy that someone can meaningfully improve. [S17]

Finding one effective engine is not the end of the work. Product-led, marketing-led, and sales-led approaches can be layered over time. Growth loops may lose effectiveness, and companies can be heavily dependent on one engine even when their growth appears diversified from the outside. Performance marketing can create cost exposure; SEO can be affected by search algorithm changes. [S8] [S9] [S15] [S16]

**Practical application (synthesis):** Continue improving the channel that works, while asking what risks come with relying on it and what other growth model may fit. Potential avenues in the evidence include user-generated templates, case studies, reviews, and product-appropriate referral mechanisms. [S14]

## A grounded next step

A useful growth review starts with three questions:

- **Value:** Are users reaching an experience that satisfies their needs, with signs such as retention or a promising loop? [S5]
- **Learning:** What hypotheses can the team test in a deliberate cycle, including ideas that may fail? [S3]
- **Durability:** Is growth built into genuine product value, and is the business preparing beyond its strongest current engine? [S2] [S8]

These principles do not establish one universal growth playbook. The supplied evidence offers examples and decision principles, but not enough to support a comprehensive 2,000-word treatment of every product, market, or growth strategy. The practical takeaway is narrower: **confirm value, experiment to learn, build on natural product-driven discovery where it fits, and diversify before one growth engine becomes a constraint.** Next step: write down one product-value hypothesis and one natural discovery opportunity, then decide how to test each.
